title: Saguache County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Saguache County the median well depth is 120 ft and median yield is 15 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost, water levels and buying land.
h1: Understanding water wells in Saguache County, Colorado
intro_html:
Saguache County covers a lot of different ground, from the San Luis Valley floor up into fractured bedrock hillsides. Well records here are extensive, with thousands of permits spread between domestic homes, stock, irrigation and monitoring wells. Depth, yield and costs change fast across short distances, so you want to read the local numbers carefully before you buy or build.

Below is what the Colorado Division of Water Resources data shows for all permitted wells in Saguache County, and how I’d use it to plan a new well or evaluate an existing one.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Saguache County
sections.html:
Across Saguache County, the median well depth is 120 feet. The middle half of wells fall between 87 and 215 feet, so a typical driller’s allowance here should cover something in that range unless you know you’re on a fringe or upland spot. About 33% of wells are shallower than 100 feet, and roughly 50% land between 100 and 300 feet. Only 12% reach 300–600 feet, and 5% go deeper than 600.

The 90th percentile depth is 400 feet, and the deepest recorded well in the county goes all the way to 4,800 feet. That tells you there are some very challenging locations. Before bidding a new well, I’d pull nearby permits around your parcel to see if you’re in a shallower alluvial area or into harder fractured bedrock.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water to expect
sections.html:
Yield numbers in Saguache County are generally solid. The median reported yield is 15 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.6 and 660 gpm. Only 5% of tested wells fall in the 1–5 gpm range, and none report less than 1 gpm, while 31% sit in the 5–15 gpm band. A full 64% of reported wells test at 15 gpm or higher.

For a single-household exempt well, you’re usually limited by the 35 gpm pumping cap long before you hit the aquifer’s capacity in the better parts of the county. Still, you should not assume “huge” irrigation production just because many wells show high test rates. Always match your expectations to the specific aquifer type and use permit on your well.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels in Saguache County are relatively shallow but have been dropping. The current median depth to water is about 30 feet, with the middle half between 15 and 60 feet below ground surface. Historical medians tell the story: around 12–14 feet in the 1960s–1980s, deepening to 20 feet in the 2000s, 30 feet in the 2010s, and 38 feet in the 2020s.

That’s a clear downward trend, meaning wells that used to have water near the surface now see it significantly deeper. It doesn’t mean you’ll run dry tomorrow, but it does matter for pump sizing and long-term planning. When you review an existing well, compare its original static level on the log with today’s measurement so you know how fast things are changing on that specific property.

sections.heading: Aquifers, geology and who is drilling here
sections.html:
Most wells in Saguache County are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 6,148 wells on record in that category. There is also heavy use of the Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifers, with 863 wells listed as “Unconfined San Luis Vall” and another 758 as “Unconfined San Luis Valley Aquifer.” Each behaves differently: unconsolidated basin fill can be very productive, while fractured rock is spottier and more site-specific.

Drilling has been steady here for decades. Permits ramped up from 309 in the 1950s and 286 in the 1960s to 1,060 in the 1970s and 1,576 in the 1990s. Activity remains strong, with 1,121 permits in the 2000s, 911 in the 2010s, and 720 already in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. Busy drillers in the records include Valley Pump Company (Self, Clinton L.), American Drilling Service (Dewberry, Bradford W.), and Authorized (Pe, Pg).

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Saguache County
sections.html:
The ground in Saguache County is a mix of sedimentary and alluvial material, and typical drilling runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 120 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $6,000–$9,000.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well commonly lands in the $12,000–$21,000 range at that depth. If your area’s nearby wells are in the 200–300 foot range rather than the 80–120 foot band, you should scale those numbers up accordingly. Before you make an offer on raw land, get copies of at least three recent well logs within a mile so you and your driller can budget realistically.

sections.heading: Risks to watch: low yield, contamination and siting
sections.html:
On paper, Saguache County looks good for yield, with no reported wells under 1 gpm and a strong median of 15 gpm. Still, fractured-bedrock areas can be hit-or-miss, and those outlier deep wells up to 4,800 feet show that dry or low-producing holes are possible in the wrong spot.

Environmental mapping shows 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 41 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles of county wells. That doesn’t mean your well is unsafe, but it does mean water testing should be routine when you buy. Plan well and septic together: keep adequate separation, respect setbacks, and factor in access for drilling rigs and future service when you lay out driveways and building pads.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Saguache County
sections.html:
County-wide, permits show 46% of wells for domestic or household use, 28% for stock, 30% for irrigation, and 8% for monitoring. That mix tells you water is heavily used both for homes and for agriculture, which matches what you see driving through areas near Center, Crestone, Moffat, Saguache and Bonanza.

When you evaluate a lot, start by pulling the well permit map and logs within a mile. Check typical depths, yields and aquifer types, and pay attention to the decade-to-decade drop in static water levels. If there’s an existing well, compare its original log to a current flow and water-level test. Then confirm your allowed uses under the permit and make sure your building, driveway and septic layout leave workable access around the well for future maintenance.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Saguache County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on Division of Water Resources records, the median well depth in Saguache County is 120 feet. The middle half of wells are between 87 and 215 feet deep. About 33% are shallower than 100 feet, around half are 100–300 feet, and a smaller share reach 300–600 feet or more. The 90th percentile depth is 400 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 4,800 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Saguache County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump tests show a median yield of 15 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between 10.6 and 660 gpm. About 31% of wells report 5–15 gpm, and 64% are 15 gpm or higher, while 5% fall in the 1–5 gpm range and none report less than 1 gpm. That’s generally plenty for a single home, but you should still test any existing well before closing.

faq.q: What is the water table depth in Saguache County?
faq.a: Static water level measurements show a current median depth to water of about 30 feet, with the middle half of wells between 15 and 60 feet. Historically, median levels were around 12–14 feet in the 1960s–1980s, deepening to 20 feet in the 2000s, 30 feet in the 2010s, and 38 feet in the 2020s, indicating a gradual decline over time.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Saguache County?
faq.a: In Saguache County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, drilling typically runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the county median depth of 120 feet, that means roughly $6,000–$9,000 for the drilled hole. A complete domestic well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical commonly totals about $12,000–$21,000 at that depth. Deeper local wells will scale those costs up.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Saguache County?
faq.a: Water quality varies by location. Records show 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 41 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles of mapped wells. Many private wells produce good water, but you shouldn’t assume. Have a full lab test for bacteria, minerals and any local contaminants of concern before relying on a well for drinking water.
